speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned with sadness this morning of the death of our colleague and friend, Harry Kuntz, member for Battle River.
Born and raised on a farm in Alberta, he had a deep respect and love for the land he represented. Although he was a relative newcomer to federal politics, his record of public service at the community level in Camrose was well established. As the father of five sons, he had an enthusiastic interest in amateur sports and volunteered his time to work with young people. Since he was elected to Parliament last year, he quickly became known among his colleagues as a dedicated constituency man. The concerns of his riding-agriculture, transportation and small business-became the concerns which he keenly pursued as a member of this House.
Mr. Speaker, I know all members will join with me in extending our sympathy to Mrs. Kuntz and her sons.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very shocked this morning to learn of the death of the hon. member for Battle River. It is always with particular sadness that one learns of the death of someone who is young in years, a husband and father of a young family.
Harry Kuntz came to the House of Commons from a part of the country where much remains of the spirit of the pioneers. He applied that spirit himself to the service of his neighbours. He was very active in the economic life of his community, in its civic affairs and, as the Prime Minister indicated, in community affairs.
His concern for the future of agriculture and the agricultural communities in his constituency was demonstrated with great sincerity and great conviction in this chamber. He was a man of very sound judgment, a man who spoke out when he had something to say. Knowing our hon. friend from Battle River, I and other members who come from other parts of the country came to appreciate the feelings and aspirations of the people he represented. I will miss his counsel.
On behalf of myself and my colleagues I join the Prime Minister in expressing our deepest sympathy to Mrs. Kuntz and her family.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in expressing our sorrow at the sudden passing of the late member for Battle River. Although Harry Kuntz had been a member of this House for only the period since the last election the seating
arrangements have been such that he was near us, physically at any rate, and my colleagues who sat close to him found him a delightful person to know. All of us wish to express our regret at his sudden and untimely passing. We extend our sympathy in particular to the Leader of the Opposition and to his party in the loss of a valued colleague.
We would ask that you, Sir, express on behalf of all of us in the House our deepest sympathy to Mrs. Kuntz and the five sons. The loss of a husband and father at such an early age is indeed a time of sadness, but we trust that the precious memories they will have through the years that lie ahead will be a source of strength and comfort to them even now.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-NATURE OF REPLY TO QUERY CONCERNING UNANSWERED ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Last Wednesday, on a point of order, I drew attention to certain questions which I have on the order paper and which have remained unanswered by the government for some time. My question of privilege arises from two things that have occurred subsequent to my raising the point of order last Wednesday.
The first is the nature of the reply made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council which I have had an opportunity to examine in Hansard and which contains what I find impossible to construe as anything other than a threat to the right and privilege of members of this House to ask questions of the government. The following were his words:

November 16, 1973
Privilege, Mr. Cossitt
I want to inform hon. members that I am attempting to find out the cost of answering these questions and on some of the more absurd ones I intend to make cost figures available.
It seems to me clear that in reality what has been said here is that members of the House should take warning not to continue asking too many questions of the government or they will be dealt with as posers of costly absurdities. There is, indeed, a not very veiled and threatening suggestion in the parliamentary secretary's remarks that members who ask questions of the government had better watch themselves or face unpleasant consequences. This sort of threatening language strikes at the acknowledged and long established duty and privilege of opposition members to examine and question in detail, without interference, any aspects of the governing of the country.
The second point on which I raise this matter of privilege arises from an article on page 41 of the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, November 15, which reported my question and the parliamentary secretary's reply. This article contains information which the writer attributes to an unnamed member of the Privy Council staff who has told him that the Privy Council has had to hire extra staff for the sole purpose of answering questions from the member for Leeds. This is an untrue, malicious and blatantly irresponsible allegation by an employee of the government to a member of the news media, and it can scarcely be interpreted as anything other than an attempt by the government through one of its bureaucrats to discredit and interfere with the right and privilege of an opposition member to examine properly matters of concern to his constituency and to the country as a whole.
In conclusion, I make no apologies for questioning this government as often as possible and, like other members on this side of the House, I will continue to exercise my right and privilege to do so regardless of direct or indirect threats to desist from a government obviously easily embarrassed when its activities are questioned.

The House, resumed, from Friday, November 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill S-4, to amend the National Parks Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I resume my remarks on Bill S-4 I am sure the House will allow me, as a member from Alberta, to express on behalf on my colleagues in that province our deep regret at the death of our colleague Harry Kuntz. We perhaps knew him best and had the best opportunity to appreciate his practicality and good advice. I would think the House would also allow these remarks because of Harry Kuntz interest in matters touched on by the bill we are discussing today, matters concerning national parks, particularly those in the north. He travelled with members of the standing committee to visit parks in northern Canada during the summer and planned to do so again. We will miss his company and his counsel.
When I began my remarks the other day, I indicated the general support members in this party have for the principles contained in Bill S-4, which is now before us, but also indicated the very grave concern we have for the lack of adequate provision in the bill as it stands for public

November 16, 1973
National Parks Act
consultation with those people who are concerned about either additions to or subtractions from the national parks in Canada. We believe substantial progress was made in the other place when an amendment was introduced and accepted requiring the printing of a notice in the Canada Gazette. We also indicated our intention to seek a more extensive provision to ensure public consultation on these matters.
The discussion of this bill in committee will provide an opportunity to review the whole national parks procedure which has caused a great deal of concern to people who have had to deal with that in the past. As the House will know, members of the standing committee will be returning to Whitehorse early in December, at which time they will have an opportunity to continue hearings there on matters relating to the establishment of parks. We had the opportunity earlier to visit the spectacular site of the new national park in the Northwest Territories. Also, as the House would know, there is very grave concern in the north about some of the boundaries of the proposed new national park in the Yukon, concern on the part of representatives of a cross-section of Canadian interests, such as wilderness groups and the native people. We hope to give them all a fair and full hearing. It would be very useful to us to have the bill before us for those purposes.
As the House knows, this bill establishes legal descriptions, and in some cases new legal descriptions, for several parks in several provinces. It also changes the status of two historic parks, Fort Beausejour and Fort Anne, and it empowers the government to establish by order in council, as a result of the intervention of the Senate, through publication of a notice in the Canada Gazette, new parks in British Columbia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Newfoundland and Ontario. We believe, as I indicated, that the amendment regarding the publication in the Canada Gazette is a significant improvement on the bill as presented to the other place.
There are some points which I wish to emphasize today. The first concerns the procedure of enshrining park descriptions in the statute, yet specifically allowing additions to national parks by order in council. This means that boundaries can be enlarged by order in council but they can only be diminished by parliament. I accept that parliament should pass on any proposal to diminish the boundaries of national parks; it is an acknowledged and welcome national responsibility of parliament to protect national parks for the enjoyment and use of future generations. However, we want an answer from the government as to why parliament should be asked to approve only diminutions of national parks. Why should we not be asked to make decisions with regard to additions? Why should that be a power that the government can exercise by order in council? Is the diminution of public land more important than the expropriation of private land? That is the principle inherent in the double standard which the government applies in this bill. It leaves citizens less protection than the state, and that is a principle about which we are concerned.
The second matter to which I would like to draw attention is the fact that this bill, as it was originally introduced in the other place, proposes that the enlargement of

public land and the expropriation of private land be achieved virtually without notice. That is unacceptable to us, as it was to the other place which introduced the amendment requiring publication in the Canada Gazette. In the testimony there, the director of Parks Canada indicated that there would be adequate safeguards by allowing groups who are interested to appear before the committees of this House and the other place. I think that the argument is a faulty one. People from distant parts of Canada will clearly not be able to come here to make the kind of representations that would be useful to committees of parliament, even if we have the time on our schedules to hear them, which we do not.
I want to point out that that argument, which the government attempted to incorporate in the bill that went to the other place, could be used to avoid public hearings on any subject. The House should note that the government's attempt to achieve this objective was stopped by the other place, which clearly possesses within its walls members who have a greater sense of democracy than does the government. As I indicated, the amendment regarding the Canada Gazette is an improvement, but we believe that the provision relative to public notice must be improved and fortified even more.
A third matter to which I would like to draw the attention of the House is the requirement in the bill for the agreement of any province to enlarge or establish national parks but it requires only consultation with the Northwest Territories. That is one more indication and affirmation of the colonial attitude which this government takes to the people who live within our Northern Territories. It is particularly dangerous coming from this government because it is clear on the record-and particularly clear on the recent record-that to this government consultation means mere advice. We would want to seriously consider and propose to the committee that the Northern Territories be treated in the same manner as the provinces, so that before parks are established in those areas there would have to be agreement rather than mere consultation.
The bill as it stands also proposes certain so-called housekeeping amendments, and principally an amendment which would allow the collection of traffic fines within the national parks. But I think it is the clear impression of members of the House, certainly members who are acquainted with the situation in national parks, that important as the question of traffic fines might be, there are several more important matters that have to be put in order in national parks. It is, of course, nonsense that matters relating to traffic fines must be referred to Ottawa now, but there is much more nonsense than that going on in the national parks as they are regulated and administered today. The committee members who came from other parts of Canada had the opportunity to visit townsites in the national parks of Banff and Jasper, and came away shocked at the colonial conditions there. They realise there is a much broader range of housekeeping matters that must be attended to, and I hope that we can attend to some of them in the committee. It is perhaps proper to ask why the government would stop to deal with the grievances of the RCMP, and not deal also with grievances of other citizens who live and work within the national parks.
November 16, 1973

I believe that the basic change which is needed in the administration and attitude of the government toward our national parks, and the people who live there, is the awareness that administration at a distance is not the best way to preserve the park values which most members in the House and most people in the townsites in the national parks know to be important. I referred earlier to the visit of the standing committee to the national parks of Banff and Jasper. Members of that committee from both sides of the House were shocked at the standard of architecture and at the look of the town of Banff. What shocked them most was the developments which had taken place under the direct control of the federal government. The reason they were undertaken is that the decisions were made at a place distant from the people who live there. By living in those places they indicate their own appreciation of the values and the beauty of the region, which is not necessarily reflected by those who live at a distance. It simply stands to reason that people who live in Ottawa and administer the parks will not be as careful about the look of a community like Banff as the people who have to live the rest of their lives in that community. It is simply one more indication of the dangers of administration at a distance which has been the underlying principle of the approach of this government to national parks.
There has been a consistent denial of self-government to the towns in the national parks. Discussions are now proceeding with the community of Banff. That does not indicate a conversion or a change of attitude; it is simply an accommodation to pressure, because extensive pressure has been applied by the residents of Jasper and Banff, as well as by the government of Alberta, in an unanimous resolution calling for a change in the approach to the administration of the two townsites. Now the government is creeping along because it knows that if it does not creep we will push it. I think members of the committee generally agree that the pace at which they are creeping now is not satisfactory, so we will push them beyond the meagre limits to which they want to go. The director of Parks Canada appeared the other night before the standing committee and refused to give a timetable for the vesting of some degree of self-government in the townsites of Banff and Jasper. I think it is very much the case that if the government is seriously interested in the housekeeping arrangements in the national parks, as indicated by the bill, we should give very high priority to self-government there. We hope that can be done.
One other aspect-and I think it is not particularly well known to people who live outside the parks-is that while the federal government keeps tight control of the right to govern which would be enjoyed in other communities outside the parks, it also keeps a tighter than usual control of the funds that are available to people who have the responsibility of administering whatever meagre powers are enjoyed by those townsites. I want to quote to the House from a letter written to me by the secretary treasurer of the Jasper school district relating directly to the grants in lieu of taxes from federal sources, which should come but which do not come to that community, from the federal government. It reads:
National Parks Act
Assessed value of federal property (at present) is $1,081,000 and at our current mill rate of 37.207 should produce $40,250.53 in grants in lieu of taxes.
Last year (1972) we received $7,970.00 grants in lieu of taxes at a mill rate of 48.085.
That is a shortfall of some $33,000 in the grants in lieu of taxes that would be paid by the federal government to a normal community. This is another example of the discrimination that is practised by the government against the residents of the townsites in the national parks.
Now I want to pass quickly to the lease situation in the townsites. There are in excess of 40 kinds of leases in operation, with the application of different terms, sometimes pertaining to the same sites. Some of these leases were imposed by duress upon the people who hold them, and the government refuses to recognize the duress that was involved. Instead, the government suggests to people who have problems that they take the matter to court, which is surely the last resort, but in this case is the only resort.
Another highly important matter that I think members of the House should be aware of, which concerns national parks, and which we might be able to consider in committee on this bill, is that there exists a very great uncertainty regarding the future of the people in the townsites within national parks and the degree to which they will be able to participate in the planning of those communities, let alone in the government of those communities.
Master plans for the townsites have been promised, and then delayed. In some communities there is a real fear that the communities themselves will be torn right by the federal government. I received a letter the other day from an executive assistant to the minister, a very alarming document, in which he expressed reservations about the right of the people in Waterton to take part in such planning. It is a dangerous precedent, I submit, for the government to suggest that the only people who have any claim of residence at all in a community have no right, because of technicalities, to participate in the planning of that community. As I say these are matters we will want to go into in more detail in committee.
Members of my party take a great deal of pride in the fact that it was a national Conservative leader who first established national parks in Canada and brought the national parks system into being. Obviously it is a distinctive and important feature of Canadian life, which allows us to maintain a respect for nature and the wilderness "for future generations".
I believe, and members on this side of the House believe that the government has taken important initiatives, some of which are outlined in this bill. We commend the minister and the government for this, but again I want to make the point that the initiatives they have taken are relatively easy initiatives. We would welcome this legislation much more if it had tackled some of the hard problems in establishing national parks in places closer to the people of Canada. Still, this bill is an important step forward. It will allow us to discuss in committee various important matters respecting the national parks system, matters that are important to the people who live within the parks. We are pleased that the bill is before us. We look forward to a

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Marchand (Kamloops-Cariboo)) introduced the second reading stage of this bill on behalf of the minister, he spent some time outlining the expansion of our national parks system which has occurred recently, an expansion which has also been mentioned by the minister, both in this chamber and elsewhere, as being a matter of great satisfaction to him. At the outset I would like to say I share that satisfaction, and I believe that the minister quite properly can take some pride in the progress that has been made in this direction since he assumed this portfolio.
For my own part, I am happy to say that both before and since the present minister took office I have believed in the desirability of expanding our national parks system, as to size and to number of parks, and over the years that I have been a member of this House I have done what I could to further that end. I just hope that the bill now before us does not represent the end of our forward movement.
The bill proposes some alterations in the method by which lands can be put into national parks. It makes provision for additions of lands to parks by proclamation of the Governor in Council, while preserving the basic concept that once lands are dedicated, as we sometimes say, to the national parks trust, they cannot be removed except by an act of the Parliament of Canada. This is a principle I can accept because there are cases when additions to existing parks are necessary and desirable, and subject to the agreement of provincial and local government authorities, I think it is reasonable that minor additions, and even possibly major additions to existing parks, could be made without having to undergo the delay involved in having legislation for that purpose introduced and passed by the two Houses of parliament.
There are two other ways in which the bill provides for additions to our park lands. One is that by proclamation certain parks which are currently, shall I say, in the process of formation, can be added to the national parks system in a formal way. One of these is currently known as the Pacific Rim Park in my constituency, a major seashore national park. This, of course, has involved negotiations with the province of British Columbia, and other parks are in the process of formation as a result of negotiations with other provincial governments.
The third proposal in the bill for the addition of lands to the national parks-and I make this distinction deliberately-is for major additions to the parks system in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I make this distinction because the lands involved in the creation of these national parks constitutionally at the present time are held in the hands of the government and the parliament of Canada.
I and my colleagues can accept all three of these proposals, with one important proviso, and one or two of my colleagues may have something to say about this aspect of the matter as the debate progresses. That proviso, Mr. Speaker, is the still uncertain status of much of these

lands in relation to the title of the aboriginal people of Canada. Of course, this has particular application at the present time with respect to the proposed national parks in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and the committee should consider it very seriously if this bill passes second reading.
The situation is not confined merely to the acquisition of park lands in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, however. It certainly is involved in the question of park lands within the province of British Columbia, and it certainly is involved in the question of lands for the parks proposed in this bill. By way of illustration, Mr. Speaker, within the proposed Westcoast National Park a number of reserves are set aside for the benefit and use of the Indian bands in that area.
In this connection, I should like to remind the House that the National Parks Act contains a provision which allows lands to be taken from the Indian people. The minister possesses this authority, but I am well aware that as far as the park to which I have made reference is concerned he has stated in writing to the Indian people that he will not use it. However, my colleagues and I have some very basic reservations about this important concept in regard to the acquisition of park lands as proposed in the bill.
"Public lands" as described in the bill, even as amended, means lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada. That is still the basic position which the minister has maintained in respect of lands within the national parks, even though they may in fact have been set aside as Indian reservations. This matter may be rectified in committee of course but I just want to say that while I approve of this bill in general on second reading, as far as this party is concerned its final passage through this House may be contingent upon resolution of that aspect.
Having indicated that I agree with expanding the area and the diversity of lands within Canada which are to be put into the national parks trust, I must say that the fact that there has been a rapid expansion in the number and diversity and location of these parks puts a particular responsibility upon members of this House to broaden the understanding of the role of national parks by the Canadian people. I think we have a clear responsibility to eliminate some of the confusion which currently exists in the minds of most Canadians regarding lands in the national parks trust, and lands which may be set aside for what is commonly referred to as recreational purposes. The hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) expressed a wish for the establishment of parks nearer to the people, and if this comes to fruition it is perhaps more important that the distinction be clearly defined than it was in the days when we only had a few wilderness parks in the Rockies.
In the case of the Pacific Rim Park, which had already achieved some status as a provincial park before the national parks were established, there is still a disposition to think of it as a place to play golf or other activities- and quite properly so-but the basic purpose of setting aside that area of the west coast of Canada was to preserve, for the enjoyment of this and future generations, some of Canada in its natural state.
November 16, 1973

The degree of misunderstanding that exists on this point is evident from the diversity of approach in the briefs submitted to the committee which was considering this subject. It brings up the related question of what steps can be taken by members of parliament individually and collectively to promote the idea of the necessity for increased recreational areas outside of the national parks system and I think we should be addressing ourselves to this key question. Indeed, the aspirations which the minister has expressed for further expansion of the national parks system are largely contingent upon a growing awareness of the system by the Canadian people.
Another matter which becomes increasingly important with the growth of national parks is the use of land immediately surrounding the parks by visitors. This immediately involves the provinces and while it may have been tentatively discussed with provincial authorities, I do not think that it has been adequately covered. The question of visitor service facilities outside the boundaries of a park is an idea which must be considered although it may not be too easy to put it into practice. This aspect is designed in part to avoid the kinds of complications which are referred to so often by the people in Banff and Jasper and by members representing those areas in this House. That is the sort of thing to which the hon. member for Rocky Mountain was just referring, and it is designed to avoid that kind of paternalistic administration which has so long characterized the life of the communities of Banff and Jasper.
In a speech that I once made following an earlier visit of the committee to Banff and Jasper, I suggested that the House should recognize that Banff and Jasper are anomalies within the national parks system which should never again be repealed. Although we recognize that because of the size and location of those parks they are useful and necessary to those who live in those particular parts, nevertheless there is a danger, and it is a very real danger which is based on my observations of Pacific Rim Park, the park which I am best able to keep under direct observation, that in the vicinity of the parks there may arise that uncoordinated sort of development which, in other localities, is described as urban sprawl.
Although that kind of development in our urban communities is considered undesirable by some, I submit that that kind of development in the territories surrounding our park is of even more serious concern, because it can ruin the parks themselves. Although the provincial authorities must of necessity be involved in this situation, I none the less urge upon the House, and I am inclined to think that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) will not quarrel with this, the idea that some of the other ministries of the federal government should concentrate on this situation to a much greater extent than has been evident up to this point. I urge that some retailoring be done with respect to some programs introduced by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion; that, possibly, the thrust of the Industrial Development Bank should be reconsidered. Indeed, it may be necessary to retailor some of the programs carried on under the aegis of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That should be done so that we can
National Parks Act
easily make available the necessary financial muscle, for the use of those who are involved in the territories immediately surrounding the parks.
While it is all very well for us to urge upon provincial authorities the need for an interrelated planning concept in keeping with the needs of the parks themselves and the development of adjacent areas, none the less, in the total picture of provincial responsibilities, the fact remains that the thrust of a national decision to spend federal tax moneys in parks may create special, and in some cases unacceptable, burdens upon agencies of provincial governments which may have direct responsibility in those areas.
If we are to get the kind of co-operation we need from provincial authorities for their agreeing to transfer to the public lands of Canada pieces of territory within existing provincial boundaries, this Parliament will have to provide a clearcut understanding as to the ancillary role which the federal authority will play in making sure that we shall avoid repeating the mistakes in other parks which we have made in Banff and Jasper. As well, we must ensure that necessary ancillary services, which in many places means appropriate recreational areas, are available in the territory adjacent to the parks.
The only other point I wish to touch on at this time, and I do so because it was raised by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, is that of self-government in the existing communities of Banff and Jasper. One need not remind hon. members of the House, especially some of those now present in the chamber, that this has long been a thorny problem. It has been a matter of great regret to me that the report of the committee of this House following the visit by that committee to Banff and Jasper in 1966-67 was, in my view, a complete whitewash with regard to existing problems of Banff and Jasper and the need for constructive solutions to them. I am rather hopeful that the present committee, after having received, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, some report on this matter from the Director General of Parks of Canada, will perhaps bring in a more constructive report, with recommendations to this House for action by the government in this area.
Really, the things which were said to committee members during the recent visit to the parks this year are not very different from the kinds of things which were said to the committee in 1966-67. However, I am pleased to note that the kinds of things which the minister's officers said to the committee were slightly different from those things which were said following the visit in 1966-67 by the then minister and his officials when they met with the committee. Although this subject matter is really not directly related to the bill before us, I think the hon. member for Rocky Mountain properly brought to the attention of the House how important and urgent the matter is. I hope that the minister, perhaps when he is closing this debate, will give some indication of the kind of thrust he hopes to see the government take in connection with this long standing problem.
I am sure that the committee will want to go into detail about the proposals for specific park boundaries, and so on, as outlined in the schedule to the bill. We shall consider that when the bill comes before the committee. I do not think we can usefully consider this at present, during the

second reading stage. Generally speaking, apart from the basic questions which I raised earlier, my preliminary observation is that, from a parks point of view, the areas which are proposed are ones which can be considered as suitable and appropriate as part of our national parks system.
Following that kind of detailed consideration by the committee, and possibly some agreement on any changes that may be desirable in the minds of the committee, hopefully we will be able to report back to the House a recommendation for the passage of this bill. However, I remind the minister that as far as the members of this party are concerned, our whole consideration of that final decision is going to be contingent in large measure upon what understanding we can reach in relation to the basic question of title to land which, according to the existing terms of the National Parks Act, are lands belonging to Her Majesty in right of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when introducing this subject to the House on November 2, the parliamentary secretary to the minister made the statement that Bill S-4, presently before us for second reading, did not incorporate any major policy changes in the National Parks Act. I have read the bill thoroughly, I have followed the debate in the other place, and I agree with the parliamentary secretary that this is the case. In my view this is the fundamental weakness of the measure. I believe new policy initiatives are long overdue.
The legislation before us contemplates the addition of new parks to the system and the alteration of some existing park boundaries. I wish to talk this afternoon about national parks policy in general and I trust that the minister, who is in his place, will also be making some observations on this subject. I am sure he agrees with everyone who has held ministerial responsibility for the national parks program that we are faced by a crisis situation calling for the wise management and multiple use of our renewable resources, a situation which can only be dealt with by comprehensive changes in government policy on park development generally. Here I am referring, of course, to the many other categories of parks outside the National Parks Act. These must be dealt with and considered if we are to meet the growing needs of our population for recreational facilities as well as the needs of a booming tourist industry.
I am delighted that at long last formal approval is being given to the acquisition of new parks. The discussions and negotiations which have been going on in this connection

have covered a period of some 15 years. When I took over responsibility for national parks in the early sixties, most of the areas covered by the legislation now before us were under discussions and consideration. As a result of renewed emphasis on national development, there was a major effort at that time to come to grips with policy initiatives on many fronts which were coordinated to deal with resource areas and development in Canada, much of which had been neglected for far too long.
The Atlantic Development Board was one of the key instruments in this regard, and it was during that time a decision was made to restore Louisburg as an historic park of some considerable magnitude at an initial cost of $9 million. The cost has, of course, increased considerably since that time because of the continuing problem of inflation in Canada. The decision to restore Louisburg is the kind of initiative that governments must take if we are to provide an adequate commemoration of our historic sites and at the same time provide some living memorials, living or animated museums so that succeeding generations will have the opportunity to actually experience the atmosphere of the highwater marks of the development of Canada as a nation.
In the area of new national parks, Terra Nova in Newfoundland became an early initiative, and later Kejim-kujik National Park in Nova Scotia. That is a tongue twister, and perhaps the reason there has been such a delay in actually getting Kejimkujik formally established is because of the difficulty in pronouncing its name. The first time I came in direct consultation with the hon. member of Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who is now the leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, was when we were undertaking negotiations which led to the establishment of this beautiful park in Nova Scotia, the second of its kind for that province, which is now being formally declared as established by the legislation before us.
The concern about northern Canada, and its lack of development, was expressed by the late Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent back in 1953 when Canada first assumed its responsibilities for the 3.5 million square miles of territory north of the 60th parallel and made it an integral part of the Canadian body politic. He used a phrase at that time which I think describes the situation quite eloquently when he said that the country had been occupied and administered in a state of absent-mindedness since confederation. A growing interest in northern development led to a consideration of the necessity of preserving some of the huge wilderness areas in the north for all future generations, and it was at that time that discussions in respect of Nahanni, Kluane and Baffin Island National Parks were commenced.
I want to pay tribute to some of the old pioneers of the north who first conceived of the notion of reserving these wilderness areas for posterity. Too often the residents of the north are accused of being only concerned with exploiting resources. The accusation has been made that those engaged in the mining industry, for example, are only interested in making a quick buck and getting out of the north. I can give evidence here today that the original suggestions for preserving national parks came from some of these pioneers of the north, the men who made it
November 16, 1973

possible for the upsurge in northern development which began under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
In addition to some of the pioneers there were newcomers, and I refer particularly to a gentleman from Baffin Island-that great and magnificent scenic wilderness up in Canada's archipelago-Mr. Bryan Pearson who originated the idea of preserving some of the scenery in Baffin Island. In fact, he pioneered in the tourist industry with a project designed to attract the attention of the jaded sophisticates from the urban communities of Canada to lure them into the high Arctic and taste some of the savage beauty of Baffin Island. He used to advertise in some of the best tourist magazines in the United States. That gentleman is now a member of the Northwest Territories Council and is still active in promoting the northern part of Canada.
I do not want to refer to each of the areas referred to in the bill. They have been under discussion for a considerable length of time and it is unfortunate that it requires so much time and that there is so much delay in implementing programs which were emergent as far back as 15 years.
There is one area not mentioned in the legislation and that is the proposed Prairie Park which has been under discussion for a number of years. I see the minister nodding his head. There is all sorts of space on the Prairies. In fact, that is the one thing of which we have most, lots of open spaces. I would have hoped that by this time the government would have negotiated with the provinces concerned in respect of a tract of land that could be preserved for all time to perpetuate the sort of sentimental nostalgia referred to in a song we sing out west quite frequently which is in part:
Where the deer and the antelope play,
Where never is heard a discouraging word,
And the skies are not cloudy all day.
There are great areas on the Prairies still available for this sort of preservation, and unless the government gets busy soon we will have_lost the opportunity to develop a typical prairie park. I am sure the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who is in the House this afternoon, will endorse what I am saying, because it was one of his visions which encouraged the minister of his day to try to get this kind of wilderness area preserved under the terms of the National Parks Act.
There is obviously a need for upgrading national parks policy. The parliamentary secretary in introducing the legislation talked about the over-use of existing parks. We used to talk about that 15 years ago. It has become chronic now. That hon. member gave the figures showing that in 1952 there were 2.5 million visitors to the parks, in 1962 the figure had more than doubled to 7.5 million, and the latest figure for 1974 is something more than 14 million visitors. Most of these people have to be accommodated in the national parks system which, with the exception of the parks mentioned in the bill before us, existed when the pressure was much less. No additions have been made to the recreational areas of Canada. I had hoped that long before now there might have been an attempt to implement a definite policy in respect of recreational parks.
National Parks Act
In 1958, the camp ground and picnic site program was initiated in co-operation with the provincial governments in order to provide adequate tourist accommodation along primarily the Trans-Canada highway system which was then under construction and, to a lesser extent, along the other major highways throughout the provinces of Canada. That program expired in 1962. We were in the process at that time of activating a program to succeed and expand the picnic site and camp ground program which would be known as the recreational parks program. Nothing transpired in this direction until the minister introduced his by-ways and highways and special places program which was announced about a year ago. The title of this program is a high-sounding phrase for a recreational parks program. There have been long delays in coming to grips with this problem. Even at the present time I am not aware of any excessive activity under the by-ways and highways and special places program.
Before there is a move into the area of recreational development, there must be consultation with the provincial governments. A relationship of trust must be established between the federal and provincial governments. This is one area in which the present government has succeeded least. It believes in a policy of confrontation rather than a policy of consultation in the area of nonrenewable resources. In the current energy crisis this has led to the impasse, which all hon. members have been made fully aware of in recent days. For the purpose of consultation and continuing discussion, a federal-provincial parks conference was established to bring together from time to time on a continuing basis the provincial resource ministers and the federal minister responsible for the national parks in order that they might work together on a comprehensive policy that would meet the growing recreational needs of the population explosion that was referred to by the parliamentary secretary.
This consultation has not continued and as a result we are faced with a crisis situation which can be resolved only by some sort of emergency response on the part of the current government of Canada. In addition to recreational parks there must be another category of park established. We must have multi-purpose parks. Many of the national parks in western Canada do not fit into the rigid structure of parks as defined by the National Parks Act. This is quite obvious in respect of Banff, Jasper, Prince Albert National Park and Riding Mountain National Park. These parks have been in existence for many years, and, because of the shortage of recreational facilities in the western part of Canada, they have assumed a multipurpose role. In his remarks the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) referred to this problem. I have been a member of at least four parliamentary committees the members of which have made pilgrimages to the mountain parks in order to try to understand what the people of those park areas want. We have made recommendations. We have urged that a special status be established for these mountain parks which obviously do not fit into the pattern.
We have urged the adoption of a principle that would preserve the wilderness concept while at the same time cater to the growing demands of the tourist population and the Canadian population which visits the western

November 16, 1973
National Parks Act
parks. However, nothing has been done in this regard. Instead there is a tendency on the part of the government, increasingly pronounced over the past ten years, to remove the facilities which are already there rather than utilizing them to the maximum and providing the recreational facilities that are required by the Canadian population today. I could refer to Riding Mountain National Park where a roller skating rink was closed down. It was located on the fringe of the park. It was a very wholesome recreational facility. It was close enough to the edge of the park so that it would not conflict with any wilderness aspect. It was arbitrarily closed down notwithstanding a strong protest from the people of Manitoba who were concerned that the taking away of this wholesome recreational facility- this was back in the 1960's, the decade of turmoil among our young people-would mean that the young people would turn to less wholesome pursuits for their recreation.
There was also an attempt to close down the church camps which provide excellent camping facilities for the young people of the province of Manitoba in Riding Mountain National Park. It was only after a massive protest by the church groups involved that the minister decided to intervene. He delayed the implementation of that policy until 1984. I do not know whether there is any significance in respect of the date 1984. It happens to be the date George Orwell referred to as the time of the takeover of all things in the Utopian state of which he wrote. I say to the minister that we must establish in concrete legislative terms a zoning policy, a multi-purpose park policy and a recreational park policy that will meet the obvious growing needs the demand for which has never been met. Because it has never been met and because of the long delay we now face a situation in which emergency legislation is necessary.
Turning again to the north which is an area in which the wilderness values I believe would be most beneficial to all the people of Canada, I might point out that there are only some 50,000 people still in the three and a half million square miles which constitute the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. I would hope that a wildlife sanctuary and a migratory water fowl sanctuary might be provided because the demand, as I believe the minister will agree, is even greater for this type of conservation activity than it is at this stage for the large national parks which are established under the legislation. It is not difficult to establish the huge areas which are marked in the legislation subject to the approval of the native people about which we have been made very conscious these days especially since the James Bay decision of yesterday which will require consultation with the native people even though it is now after the fact.
We also need wildlife and wild bird sanctuaries. The Wood Buffalo National Park fits largely into this category because it is there that the large herd of wood buffalo is preserved for posterity and also where the whooping crane, a species that came during the decade of the 1950's near to extinction, with only 23 birds remaining, finds a breeding ground. During the early 1960's public interest in the whooping crane became phenomenal, one of the major conservation issues. Eggs were flown south to hatching

grounds in the southern United States where the birds winter, and still, as far as we can determine, the population of this beautiful white bird has not reached more than 42 in its natural habitat. Were it not for the Wood Buffalo National Park, the species would be even more threatened as it makes that hazardous flight of 3,000 or 4,000 miles across the happy hunting ground of the Prairies and still manages to survive. This is the sort of thing that is needed in greater abundance in the northern regions of Canada.
To bring my remarks to a conclusion, I want to refer to the necessity of co-ordinated intergovernmental action in order to accomplish what must be accomplished urgently in the parks policy and in all these other conservation matters to which I have referred briefly this afternoon. In 1962 the Resources for Tomorrow Conference took place in the city of Montreal. In the light of what is happening today with the crisis in energy and so forth, even the title of that conference is prophetic today. Some 1,000 concerned Canadians met in the Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal to bring their collective wisdom to bear on the problem of the threatened renewable resources, and since that time the renewable resource area has become a matter of prime concern to governments at all levels. But I remember in 1962 it was rather an "in" joke to laugh at a government that was occupied with the conservation of water resources-such a colourless subject when Canada had an abundance of water. In fact, I believe that the phrase used by one of the pundits of that day was that we had water running out of our ears.
It is only eleven years later, but we are all aware now that we are faced with problems of wisely managing our renewable resources. When I say "managing" I do not mean to put a lid on it. We had a positive attitude toward renewable resources. It was managing in such a way that they would be constantly renewable, and we are still far from achieving this high ideal.
Out of that conference, a Resource Ministers Council emerged which was to meet regularly to co-ordinate provincial and federal policy because of the problems of divided jurisdiction. That council did not receive the backing of the governments that have been in office from 1963 to 1968 and from 1968 until the present time, with the result that it has fallen into disuse and is now completely abandoned, so I understand. It might rise from the ashes under a new heading because there is a tendency of the government to re-issue old policies and put their own particular stamp upon them.
I will close with the admonition of the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark). If we are going to meet the demands and the challenges in the park area in the renewable resource area, it can only be achieved by continuous consultation, not token consultation. There was an attempt to decentralize the administration of the parks in 1962/63 and regional offices were established across Canada. Recently, two additional offices-originally there were three offices-have been established, one in Winnipeg and another in Quebec city. But the establishment of regional offices will serve no useful purpose unless there is a decentralization of authority, unless there is some local autonomy in this area. If the regional offices that have been established, and this has been the pattern over the past ten years, are merely a vehicle through
November 16, 1973

which the people in the areas concerned and the provincial authorities have to approach the summit in Ottawa, it complicates the process of consultation rather than facilitates it, and this has been the pattern that has developed.
I would urge the minister to give some real autonomy to these regional offices and to let them consult with the people who are concerned. Theirs is a positive concern, not a selfish or negative concern. The message now is accepted by all serious minded Canadians that we have to manage our renewable resources wisely, and if the message has not come through loud and clear to this point, the trials and tribulations through which we are passing at present because of the government's failure to come to grips with the resource policy will bring the message home to every Canadian loud and clear. This legislation is going to the committee and I hope that we have a thoroughgoing discussion on the broader issues. This is a housekeeping bill when we should be having a major breakthrough in parks policy after these long years of delay. 1 am hoping that after we are through with the bill in the committee some amendments will be adopted which will help to put some teeth into the legislation, particularly in the consultative process. Unless we bring all the people of Canada together in support of a comprehensive resource policy we will not get anything more than we have here this afternoon, namely the formal legislative approval, to discussions, negotiations, and actions that have been under way for at least 15 years. Governments which wish to cope successfully with the challenge must move much more quickly than that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks today will be of very short duration. First I would like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Kuntz) whose tragic death we mourn today. I would like to pay tribute to him especially because he was very active in the northern affairs committee, was very concerned about national park matters, and played a real role this summer when we visited many of the national parks. We certainly mourn his passing.
I would like to divide my remarks about the parks into two sections, and as I said they will be short. The first has to do with the role of the Indian people in the parks. I am concerned especially about the Pukaskwa National Park, which is not mentioned in this bill. It is a park about which negotiations are going on right now, and is located on the north shore of Lake Superior.
There is the problem that arises when we take the rules under which we operate our parks and apply them to an area where our native people have been living for tens of thousands of years. We have records in that area showing that native people have been there for 10,000 to 15,000 years. Perhaps it is improper for me to say that a people are part of the environment, but in discussing Indian people we have to look at them really as people who are part of the environment. They know their environment, they understand it, and they live in it.
To say we are creating a park to preserve the environment, and then remove the Indians from that park, not allowing them to hunt or fish in it, is ridiculous. The native Indian people of Canada still feel strongly about
National Parks Act
their environment, and when we understand that then we can see the ridiculousness of the situation. There is a growing movement among native peoples to look back, to meet with their elders, to talk to the wise people and to the medicine people. More and more the young people are getting together with the medicine people and are studying their way of looking at the environment. Traditionally when an Indian killed a deer he did so for one reason, and that was for food. He also honoured the deer when he killed it. We have to learn about their attitude to the environment. One of my good friends, an ecologist, a top man in his field, says that the original ecologist is the Indian.
I am not satisfied when I hear our national parks people talking about making a deal with Indians so that in some way we can recompense them for taking away their freedom to hunt and live in the parks. That is not adequate. We have to be very concerned about the Indian people in a park like Pukaskwa-and I know there are others across the country-where they are part of the environment, and whose traditional life should not be disturbed but encouraged. They have a role to play in that park in terms of continuing to live in the manner in which they have for thousands and thousands of years.
The other point I wish to make concerns something quite different, namely, the communities of Banff and Jasper. They are two anomalies in our parks, but nevertheless they exist, have existed for many years, and will continue to exist as communities. There is no doubt about that. There is no question of their disappearing. They are very viable communities, but communities which are in a great deal of trouble. I think the most characteristic thought you get when you visit Banff concerns crowding. It is tremendously crowded. Far too many people are living in a small space. It lacks planning and cohesion. There is a great need for more space, and I think the extra space should be provided not at Banff itself but around Canmore. Jasper is not so crowded, but it, too, lacks planning. It does not know where it is going.
Both communities have one central problem to which we as parliamentarians must direct ourselves. All citizens of this country, no matter where they live, should have the right to govern their own affairs within their own community. A community cannot exist if its citizens do not have the right to make their own rules to govern themselves. This is something that is lacking in both these communities. One of the citizens of Jasper said to me that he has only one vote, and that that vote is for the federal representative, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark). This is not to say that he is not doing a good job. I think he is doing a fine job for those communities, but the fact remains that the citizens of those communities have only one vote. They do not have a provincial vote or a municipal vote. In effect, they have no mayor and no provincial member. They have a federal member of parliament and that is it. They are denied other representation because they live in a national park. The point I wish to make is that both these communities must be given some kind of status within the parks, and be given it soon before lack of planning destroys these communities and the respective parks completely.

November 16, 1973
National Parks Act
One other point I would like to mention about Jasper is that it is a railroad centre. A great deal of thought should be undertaken before any move is made to remove the railroad and railroaders from Jasper. I would be very concerned if any efforts were made to remove this turn around point without first having the utmost consultation with the people involved, with the railroad unions, and with the railroads. It is something that should be examined carefully. Having visited Jasper many times I see no reason why the railroad should not stay there and, as I say, before any steps are taken to remove the railroad considerable examination and consultation should be undertaken.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to make only a brief intervention in this debate on the bill to amend the National Parks Act. I do so for two reasons. One is that I am genuinely interested in national parks and in their importance to our national life. The second is that the Prince Edward Island National Park lies mostly within my constituency, and I am especially interested in it. The Prince Edward Island Park is one of our smallest national parks, embracing only something like 150,000 square miles, yet over one million people visit it in the course of a year, which represents an extremely high use for this small area of land. Although this is very commendable, it also creates special problems.
In his speech introducing second reading stage the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Marchand (Kamloops-Cariboo)) said, as recorded at page 7494 of Hansard:
The second important purpose of the bill is to allow future additions to existing national parks to be achieved by proclamation, thus avoiding the necessity of having to introduce new legislation for each such change. The other clauses amending the National Parks Act are basically administrative and updating.
To me this is an important procedure on which we are embarking because we are removing from Parliament control over changes in park boundaries. Changes can now be made as an administrative function, eliminating the role of the member of parliament as a representative of the area affected. Although I am in favour of this because it is necessary from the point of view of efficiency, it places upon the administrators a special responsibility to be extremely sensitive to the desires and will of the people affected by the changes they make. Local relationships are extremely important in matters like this. My caution applies with special force to the Prince Edward Island National Park because it is located in a relatively high density population area. Our greatest resource in Prince Edward Island is land, but this resource is limited so we must make sure that we use every bit of it to the best advantage. When these extra powers are put in the hands of the park administrators they have, therefore, a special responsibility to make sure that their actions meet with the approval of the local people.
In one sense, as the previous speaker pointed out, a national park is a local residence and everything that takes place there affects the local environment and the people who have been living there for generations perhaps. I would urge that the minister impress upon his officials the importance of maintaining rapport and an

excellent relationship with the people who live in the area of the park and who would be affected by any changes. While I have a great respect for experts, Mr. Speaker, I have a deeper respect for the innate knowledge of the local people. I believe there is a duty on the park administration to ensure that what looks fine on paper in some high rise office in Ottawa, makes sense when it is applied in a local area thousands of miles away. The parks administrators should make it a practice to take local people into their confidence, and to seek the advice not only of provincial governments but also of local governments and the individuals and associations concerned.
A case in point is the Prince Edward Island National Park. I am not in a position to judge the validity of the criticism or anything else, but apparently the park administration decided-and perhaps for good reason- that the very famous Green Gables golf course should be reconstituted and redesigned. They propose to subtract some land from the course, then buy other land to replace what has been removed. Hundreds of people were shocked and amazed at this action. There are two possibilities here: one is that the action was sensible and the other is that it was really necessary; but if such is the case it has not been properly explained to the people. I hope this is not being done just because of an administrative whim; perhaps they should have left it the way it was even if it were not so neat from an administrative point of view.
Another example might be given concerning that same national park which involved the intense use of land and the local facilities. The Stanhope school stands cheek by jowl with the national park. Two or three other local schools were added to it. Control over private property in the immediate area was lost, perhaps due to lack of suitable zoning by the provincial government, and so there is a great increase in the number of children but there is no proper playground for them. A request was made for a little bit of parkland to be used as a playground on a temporary basis. I do not know the outcome of this request, but I am sure the minister will give it sympathetic consideration.
I should like to cover two other points, Mr. Speaker. I agree, of course, with the change in the name of the park to Prince Edward Island Park from Prince Edward Park. In the bill there is an appendix which describes the new boundaries of the park in technical and legal terms in five sections; I would suggest to the minister that maps should be provided when the bill goes to committee in order that the proposed change in the boundaries of the Prince Edward Island National Park may be easily understood. I recognize the necessity for legal description, but it is meaningless to people not thoroughly familiar with the area.
I should like to reiterate how important it is for the park administration to realize that, in one sense, a park is a legal residence; it has to fit into the local community. Any action that the administration takes should be in harmony with the will, the desires and the activities of the area in which the park lives, so to speak.
November 16, 1973

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you can rest assured that I am quite pleased to participate in the debate on Bill S-4, which we are called to pass on second reading and whose objectives are as follows: first, to include Kejimkujik and Forillon in the national parks system; second, to authorize the Governor in Council to set aside by proclamation lands for eight additional national parks, including St. Maurice, and third, to extend, by proclamation, existing national parks without having to resort to a legislative measure in each case.
The most important aspect of this bill, as regards the province of Quebec, is obviously the establishment of two parks in that province, namely Forillon and St. Maurice.
It is not the first time that I speak about the establishment of a national park in Quebec, more specifically in the Gaspe Peninsula, as I advocated in my maiden speech delivered in this House in 1963.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
-and also your colleague from
Bonaventure.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
In this regard, I say that I have always been seconded by my colleague and friend from Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine.
I knew then that such a tremendous project could not be achieved overnight. However, I also knew that if the project were approved in the near future, the citizens living near the park and Gaspe people generally would be very happy to benefit from the many advantages deriving from such a park.
Following that I continued to make representations to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development as well as the secretary for the province of Quebec. That was done only within the framework of the Canada-Quebec agreement for the development of the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe area. Section 55 of that agreement provides that Canada would undertake the development of a park in the Forillon Peninsula. The province of Quebec would take it upon itself to purchase the land and hand it over under a lease free of encumbrances to the government of Canada for a period and on terms acceptable to both parties.
As a follow up to that original agreement on May 26, 1968, negotiations took place between the two governments and I would like here to commend the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and pay tribute to the courageous minister as well as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), formerly in charge of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, for bringing those negotiations with the province of Quebec to a conclusion.
In the agreement of May 26, 1968, it was agreed that the province would undertake to take the necessary steps before December 31, 1970, to free the lands from all possible encumbrances or acquire their ownership free of encumbrances, inform the government of Canada as the said lands are released or acquired and give free tenure of

the said lands to the government of Canada before December 31, 1970.
That is one of the obligations of the province of Quebec under that agreement. On the other hand, the government of Canada makes the commitment that the development and administration of that park will fully reflect the linguistic duality in Canada and more specifically the French characteristic of the province of Quebec and the Gaspe area. On the other hand, Quebec has agreed to have a utilization plan prepared for the pieces of land bordering on the park, while respecting its objective, natural beauty and fine qualities. The lease is for a 99 year term; however, there is a provision in the agreement whereby Quebec may, following a 60 year period, purchase Forillon Park from the Canadian government by reimbursing all capital expenditures which the central administration may have incurred.
Mr. Speaker, in the annex to this agreement appear all the amounts which must be spent during the period from 1970 to 1976-77, that is a total of $8,887,000 for the development of this park by the federal government.
Present and future economic benefits of such a park for the area are indeed numerous. Already, since the development operations of the park began in 1973, it has provided jobs for 175 Gaspesian residents. Last year's budget for Forillon Park totaled $2,500,000 and no change is expected this year. In wages alone $823,000 were paid last year to the park employees in that region. To this amount you can add the capital input of tourists. The park is obviously an incentive and a monetary input for the region directly involved, mainly the Forillon peninsula.
In 1972, the first year of operations, 84,726 visitors were recorded and their number increased to 165,000 in 1973. At the current rate, as someone said several years back at the time of the establishment of the park and as stated by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), Forillon Park should receive over 600,000 visitors.
As early as 1976, Forillon Park will become a genuine wildlife museum extending over 92 square miles.
Through the National Park Act which is aimed at ensuring the perpetual conservation as national inheritance of the regions containing important geographical, geological, biological or historical elements, the Forillon peninsula, by its history and situation, is an intouchable entity of this patrimony. Its 92 square miles and its varied natural elements surrounded by the sea are a splendour which no Canadian can ignore during a Gaspesian trip.
For true nature lovers and for the amateurs of natural sciences and the geologists or botanists, as well as for the historic peculiarity enthousiasts, Forillon Park will become a sort of museum of wilderness which will exhibit in their original surrounding the remains of prehistoric civilizations, the remains of ancient Micmacs camps, a lead mine opened by Superintendant Talon in 1758 and, offshore, ships sank by the Kirke brothers in 1628.
This park also includes Fortune Fort, an underground fort built during World War II to protect the Gaspe Bay against German submarines. This fort was restored last year.
November 16, 1973

Forillon National Park is also a sanctuary for several species of game animal, sea birds, birds of prey and marine mammals. Common and grey seals have also been observed in the territorial waters of Forillon Park from mid-May to the end of December. Their arrival seems related to a biological factor, the young being born around this period.
Now I should not want to use all my time as I know that several members wish to add their comments. It would take hours to describe the wonders of Forillon Park but, Mr. Speaker, I would like to report to this House for the first time and announce publicly also for the first time in Canada a discovery we made this summer in the park. We found in Forillon Park the white headed eagle called the bald eagle and I quote a report prepared on the subject.
We observed that bird on June 4 and September 9, 1972. In both cases the weather was clear and it was easy to make a positive identification. In June 1937, Ball (1938) observed one of those eagles at Grande-Greve.
Mr. Speaker, this is to give you an idea of the fauna, birds of prey and game we find in Forillon National Park.
