subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the government for bringing forward this bill to regulate our national parks. It is about time it was brought forward. These parks have been under consideration for a long time and this is a matter we should deal with in the House of Commons. I bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that a speech made in this House by the minister's parliamentary secretary and printed in Hansard was circulated throughout the country. Unfortunately for the people of Canada, the minister felt that should be done. It is that kind of thing which runs the cost of government up and up and up. If a minister makes a speech in the House of Commons, it is not fair if he uses his departmental budget to circulate the speech across the country. Like any member, he has the right to purchase copies of Hansard, but it is an abuse of the money set aside to run the department if a minister uses a speech which he
National Parks Act
or his parliamentary secretary makes in this House as a method of propaganda.
I want to comment on one clause in this bill that bothers me. It has also been included in other bills which have come to this House. I refer to clause 3 which provides a criminal sanction against those who use the park-in a sense a new form of criminal law that activates within national parks and is created by the governor in council making regulations. I would not be so concerned about this except that it is the duty of parliament to make laws, especially laws which affect the rights and freedom of our citizens.
For too long we have allowed government, through some nameless bureaucrat, to produce regulations which somehow get pushed through the Privy Council office and approved by the governor in council. The new statutes thus created penalize people and amount to a new type of criminal law. Ordinary citizens can incur penalties imposed, almost at the whim of someone employed by government, because he has broken laws which have never been debated in this House or considered by the justice committee.
The particular provision which bothers me provides that for breaking these rules-rules which do not even exist so far-a person may be denied access to a park for up to five years. I wish to draw to the attention of the House the fact that major national highways pass through certain of our parks-those at Gaspe and Banff come immediately to mind-and it could easily happen that a person could be denied the right to traverse a park solely because some bureaucrat had made a rule or had been out to get him.
There is, of course, a need for regulation with regard to conduct in national parks. We must get tough with the polluter and the despoiler, the person who hacks the trees and leaves garbage around. But surely these rules governing the use of the parks can be brought by the Minister to the House for final determination, as is the case with any other criminal sanctions which apply throughout the country. As an illustration of what so often happens under the present system, I would refer hon. members to the rule which the National Capital Commission has made imposing a speed limit on the new route to the Ottawa airport. A new expressway has been constructed, yet a speed limit of 40 miles an hour has been imposed, one which is almost totally unenforceable and constitutes nothing more than a speed trap, for no reason whatsoever.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
This is the sort of thing that goes on when bureaucrats who are not subject to election make rules and laws. This kind of thing constitutes an abuse of the rights of the people of Canada. I read with interest the statement made by the parliamentary secretary at the opening of the debate. I wish to bring the attention of hon. members to one paragraph of that statement in which the hon. gentleman said:
This brings us to the immediate and future needs of Canadians living in cities and growing urban centres who want, and need, easy and quick access to recreational land.

November 16, 1973
National Parks Act
Unfortunately, this is all he says on the subject. He simply says he recognizes that Canadians in urban areas need ready access to recreational land. And he says nothing else. I regret that neither the minister nor his parliamentary secretary are here. Perhaps they will read Hansard. I should like to bring it to their attention that more than 80 per cent of the people of Canada will shortly be living in urban areas. It is all very well for us to establish national parks to reserve and preserve the national heritage of Canada, but a great many of these parks are totally inaccessible to the vast majority of the population.
While it is necessary for us to preserve the Virginia falls and the ice-caps of Baffin Island, I must say it doesn't do my constituents much good. I suppose this is equally true of those who live in most of the other constituencies represented in this chamber. We must tackle the real problem which the burgeoning urban growth of Canada is presenting. In 1952 a hurricane destroyed the lives and property of a great number of people in metropolitan Toronto. It is an ill wind that does not blow some good for someone. As a result of that hurricane, conservation and flood control measures were financed by the government of Canada. Certain parks were created. If hon. members go to those parks on a fine day in summer, they will find it very difficult to get in. By ten or eleven o'clock in the morning the gates would probably be closed. This is because there is such a pressing demand for parks around our great cities.
I shall be parochial for a while and refer to the great city of Toronto and the golden horseshoe area. We are in a difficult position because our recreational land, our wilderness land is to a large extent to the north in the shield country and it takes at least an hour, possibly two hours, to reach it. Unlike Montreal and Vancouver, there is no open land relatively close to our city. The province of Ontario has recognized this situation and has proposed a parkway belt around Toronto. It has also proposed to create parks of fairly significant size in and around the city. The intention is to freeze development and purchase as much as possible of the Niagara escarpment.
Unfortunately, while Ontario is treated as a wealthy province, when you get right down to it the reason they cannot acquire that parkway belt, the reason they cannot acquire the Niagara escarpment and assemble the recreational resources so urgently needed by those who occupy apartment buildings and townhouses, is that they do not have the dough. Hon. members may ask why this should be so. One of our problems is that the province of Ontario is rich and it pays 50 per cent of the total cost of the national government; and the great bulk of this contribution comes from the golden horseshoe area. I suggest that our contribution to the national revenue exceeds that made by all the industries and businesses in the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext: What do you get back for it?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member asked that question, because we get back very little in terms of what can be done for the people who create the wealth of this nation. One of the things those who create the wealth need is a place to relax, to get out of the smog and breathe fresh

air. Maybe the smog results from our creating wealth, but somewhere along the line we must recognize that the people who work must have a place where they can relax, enjoy themselves and get some fresh air into their lungs. This is an important national interest and it is a matter in which this government should take a keen interest when considering a new parks policy. Not only do we need a new parks policy to reserve and preserve the beautiful and the historic but we need a policy designed for the purpose of providing recreation close to areas where our people work and live. Such a parks policy would cost a great deal of money. Recreational land is at a premium already and is being snapped up by people who build elaborate establishments, put fences around them and hang "No trespassing" signs on the fences. They sometimes even have a big dog and put up signs telling people to beware.
I suggest that farmland is being picked up in this fashion and the price is getting higher and higher. Very soon there will not be enough land left for the purpose of recreation. This is a serious matter and it is imperative that governments begin to consider the problems of people in the cities who want to get away on occasions to hike, ride bicycles, operate snowmobiles, fish or do other things of a recreational nature.
One might suggest that we build another Highway 401 or 400 so that people can drive 150 or 200 miles away from the cities, perhaps up to areas like Temiscamingue, but we have problems such as shortage of fuel and insufficient time. We must build recreational resources close to where people work and live. I urge the government to get together with the province of Ontario to work on this matter. The Niagara escarpment would be a beautiful place to preserve as a national park. Perhaps it could run from the escarpment or from Niagara Falls back through the gorgeous rocky rim to the trees and the bush along the Bruce Peninsula. But this cannot be done without money and without a government which is prepared to come to grips with urban problems.
Members of this House must pay attention to urban problems and the needs of the people living in urban areas. The province of Ontario is attempting to freeze or hold back development, but holding bylaws are of no real value because people build bigger establishments and bigger fences and then we have to expropriate the land at a much higher price. It is imperative that the national government recognize this as a national priority and get together with the province of Ontario or its conservation authority to build national parks close to where people live. This involves areas of high taxes and perhaps great wealth, but these are the areas of central Ontario which have a tremendous need for recreational facilities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on Bill S-4 coming from the Senate. I have always spoken in favour of the conservation of our natural resources, the preservation of our environment in its natural state.
As most other members, I had the opportunity to visit several national parks throughout Canada and we from New Brunswick are particularly proud to have Fundy National Park among the national parks as it will soon be
November 16, 1973

the case of the new Kouchibouguac Park which is the subject matter of this bill.
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker, the member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) has made, in my opinion, a quite valid criticism of the provincial government which does not seem to have any logical policy for the development of its parks. It undoubtedly shows a division between the federal and provincial wings of that party and I hope that the Tory members of Ontario will succeed in reconciling their views on the matter.
Mr. Speaker, the member for Peel South has also mentioned that the hard-working Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and his parliamentary secretary had distributed throughout Canada a great many copies of the excellent speech which the parliamentary secretary delivered in this House on November 2.
I find that there again it is perhaps a matter of petty and parochial politics. If we stop to consider, for instance, that the parliamentary secretary to the minister was the first Indian elected to the House of Commons, that the minister has honoured him by asking him to pilot this bill in the House, it does seem to me that it is hardly the right time for an hon. member issued from the first citizens of this country to start playing party politics.
Nevertheless, the speech to which I listened two weeks ago was one of the best I ever heard and I recommend its wide distribution across the country.
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us gives us the opportunity to speak in favour of our own area, our parish, if I may say
so.
Of course, I support the bill and I feel bound to say at the outset that there is no problem here. As the parliamentary secretary put it, it is a milestone but an important one in the development of a national parks system throughout the country in the framework of a consistent national policy.
In Madawaska, people wonder whether a national park should be developed. They have been wondering about it for many years now. I might outline to my colleagues the geographical context that I am referring to. Madawaska was one of the first areas of New Brunswick to be settled. I shall not dwell on the circumstances which led Acadians, and later on Canadians from Quebec, to settle in that area. Anyway, the St. John River flows through this area and some 250 miles downstream into the Bay of Fundy.
Two major streams flow into the St. John River; on the one side, in the state of Maine, there is the Allagash River, which the Americans have tried to preserve in its natural environment, and on the other side, rolling down from the province of Quebec, there is the Saint-Frangois River. As there are many rivers with that same name in Quebec, I wish to specify that I am referring here to the one which forms, here and there, along the border between Canada and the United States, a chain of lakes in a natural environment that is most picturesque and virtually inaccessible, except by way of a rough country road that we have been trying to improve lately.
National Parks Act
Mr. Speaker, that area formed, in the early days of the settlement, an extremely large unit, not a political unit but a community of interests, on account of the background of its inhabitants, who were Acadians, and therefore Frenchspeaking. Later on people from Boston, Connecticut and other areas, following the American wars also settled in the area.
Now, in 1842, the Madawaska area was brutally divided into two parts, by the Ashburton-Webster treaty, negotiated by Lord Ashburton from England and Daniel Webster, of notorious renown for some reasons in the United States. The Madawaska community was thus divided into two parts and that division still exists and one should not be surprised for instance to find out that the vast northern section of the state of Maine is mostly inhabited by French-speaking people. I point out that Madawaska is also, of course, of French origin.
However we warmly welcome all people who come to visit us, or live with us regardless of their ethnic origin. This is the attitude that prompted us from time to time, through a gesture that has nothing to do with folklore but comes from a longstanding tradition, to proclaim the existence of the Republic of Madawaska.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the minister, as I have already done in writing a few years ago, to consider the advisability of developing an international park in this area enclosed by three borders, that of New Brunswick, that of Quebec and that of the United States. We have international parks in Canada that are more or less important according to their origins.
But as for us, the people from Madawaska, who have been historically denied some of our rights, who have lost a large part of a territory that we were traditionally claiming, we would readily accept a gesture of reconciliation on the part of the Canadian and the American authorities as well as the government of the province of Quebec, namely the establishment of an international park in the River Saint-Frangois area.
Mr. Speaker, as time is running fast, I will put an end to my remarks. I simply wish to give the minister the friendly warning that I intend to submit this proposal in the future, whether in this House, in committee or in private, because the minister has much sympathy for me and for all representations from the Republic of Madawaska. Therefore, I will only ask today, perhaps for the first time in this House, that an international park, a tri-border park, be established in our beautiful part of the country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks in respect of Bill S-4 which is before us. As a rookie in this House I find it rather strange that the bill should come from what I often hear referred to as the other place. Be that as it may, there are several points I should like to make.
First, I am very happy to see a bill before this House which gives us an opportunity to discuss the question of parks. If I had my way, the whole of the Northwest Territories would be a park and all the people here would be invited to visit us once in a while. I have found from my travels throughout Canada that many white people also like the idea of parks. They have to struggle in a

November 16, 1973
National Parks Act
concrete jungle for nine or ten months of the year, or more, and enjoy spending a few weeks in the hill country living something like the Indian people.
There are two particular points I should like to mention. I hope hon. members will bear them in mind when this bill is studied further and comes to a vote. One involves clause 10 which refers to agreement being reached with the province concerned that the lands to be set aside are suitable for a national park. Clause 11 provides:
The governor in council may, after the consultation with the Council of the Yukon Territory or the Council of the Northwest Territories, as the case may be, by proclamation, set aside as a national park of Canada, under a name designated therein-
I am a little concerned about the words "after consultation" because of previous experience in respect of consultation in the Northwest Territories. The consultation, to say the least, has been very poor. There is a danger inherent in this clause, as I see it, which could cause some worry especially to the native people of the Northwest Territories who at present are preparing a position to place before the government to the effect that there may not be any land to claim if the parks are set up by proclamation. That is one point I wish to make which I should like hon. members to bear in mind, that is, that the question of land settlement has not been settled in the Northwest Territories.
There are also questions in respect of the hunting and fishing rights of the people in the Northwest Territories. These rights must be protected. I do not believe the National Parks Act at present protects the hunting and fishing rights of the native people of the Northwest Territories. This must be borne in mind when one discusses the idea of national parks for both the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories.
In order to point out the importance of hunting and fishing to the people of the north, I should like to refer to one or two statements made to me not too long ago. A chief from the area of Fort Franklin was quite concerned about hunting and fishing rights being eroded as a result of legislation in other parts of the country. He said that the white man has his bank, and that when things get tough he can go to the bank, write a cheque and receive the money necessary to buy groceries in order to keep going until things are better. The chief said that he did not have a bank in this sense, but that his bank is Great Slave Lake or Great Bear Lake where there are plenty of fish. He said that when things get tough and he needs a food supply for his family and his dog team, it is there. That is his bank and he would like to have it protected.
Another matter concerns the employment of native people in the parks across the country. I do not know how good the record is, but I would point out the experience of two chiefs from the Northwest Territories who visited our national parks four or five years ago. After visiting some of the parks they returned to the territories and said that the people of the south desperately needed parks because their lands were being used for other purposes; therefore land should be set aside for their recreation and that of future generations. They said they did not see any Indian people employed in the parks. They did not even see any who were visitors to the parks. They said that the only Indians they saw near a park were two outside the park
who had to pay to enter it. That did not leave a very good impression.
I should also like to refer to a comment made by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) who suggested that it would cost a great deal of money to acquire land and operate parks in Canada. I would mention the fact that before the coming of the white man this whole country was a park and my people ran them on total unemployment. We might examine this question with a view to reinstating that idea. The Indian people, being some of the great socialists of this country are, I believe, also some of the greatest park keepers this country has ever known.
Briefly, those are some of the points I wanted to make and I hope hon. members will bear them in mind when this bill goes to committee and comes up for a vote.

I wish to echo the words of hon. members who spoke before me, specifically the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), and the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). I realize that wide-open spaces are very nice and I wish I could be there, living as I do so close to Edmonton, but this raises a point on which I wish to comment.
There is a small provincial park a couple of miles from my home. It is 15 miles from Edmonton. Almost any day of the week when you go past that park during the summer, you find an overabundance of trailers and people in it. Therefore, I think there is a great need for the federal government to find a way of financing small recreational-type parks within easy reach of people living in the cities.
A number of problems are tackled in the bill before us, such as the consideration of new park boundaries, the addition or deletion of the boundaries of parks and the administration of the parks. Because this bill outlines such housekeeping activities in parks as the collection of fines and traffic control, it opens up the whole question of self-government of the townsites in the national parks.
Although there is no national park within my riding, I am aware of the necessity for control of the internal administration of townsites by the people who live in them. Surely it is one of the principles of democracy that people living in a town should have jurisdiction and control over the traffic in that town, the repair and upkeep of its streets, the disposal of sewage and the proper development of the town. Surely people in townsites such as Jasper, Banff and Waterton have the right to self-government. However, I should like to caution the minister on one point before he grants self-government to these town-sites, and that is that there should be full consultation with the inhabitants.
I might add to what was said by the hon. member for Northwest Territories that in many cases the government does not seem to have the word "consultation" in its

November 16, 1973

dictionary. However, I have confidence in the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) because his answers appear to be straightforward and I believe he will engage in full consultation with the towns if he has in mind giving them self-government in the future. I would add that he might consider increasing grants, which the hon. member for Rocky Mountain has described as being pitiful, in lieu of taxes. I hope that in the future these townsites will receive the $33,000 which they seem to think should be coming to them.
Coming as I do from a small town in the riding of Wetaskiwin, I know that people are trying to escape the urban sprawl and migrate to smaller communities so that they can enjoy country life, what they call the good life. I think it is necessary for the minister to consider people who have residences within the townsites, who do not live there the year round but only come to them for the scenery or for skiing once or twice a year. Because of the great shortage of housing in the townsites of Banff and Jasper-I am aware of this because I was a member of the committee which went to those townsites and heard the people voice this problem-the minister said that he would provide trailers as a temporary measure to alleviate the problem. I understand, however, that he has had a change of heart. I hope that people who have lived in these areas for generations will be allowed to build houses there.
A point that was brought to my attention and which I believe should be mentioned is that there are no old-age homes within the townsites of Jasper and Banff. I may be wrong, and if so I stand to be corrected. However, I think it is totally wrong that people who have lived all their lives in these areas should have to go to Edmonton or other cities in their old age. I would like the minister to take this matter into consideration and provide the necessary facilities.
It is close to four o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude now.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks I should like to express my appreciation for the way in which my motion was received by the House last Wednesday. It required the unanimous consent of members of the House for this debate to take place on the joint communique issued by the members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and the European parliament. It was granted, and I appreciate that very much.
My main purpose in bringing this matter before the House is to focus the attention of hon. members on an aspect of Canada's foreign relations which it seems to me has not been considered seriously enough. I am referring

November 16, 1973
Communique of Canadian and European Parliaments to Canadian relations with the European Economic Community, the EEC of the EC as it is now called. As many hon. members are aware, a delegation from the European parliament was in Ottawa from October 31 to November 1 of this year. This was the first formal contact between the parliament of Canada and the European parliament, a fact which is rather surprising when one considers that the Treaty of Rome creating the original six-member EEC was signed as long ago as 1957.
It is appropriate that I mention how this first formal contact came about and how the two committees became involved. When the committee on foreign affairs of the other place undertook an examination earlier this year of Canada's relations with the European Community, they visited the Community headquarters in Brussels for several days and had an informal meeting with a delegation of the European parliament chaired by Mr. Peter Michael-Kirk, a British MP and chairman of the Conservative group in the European parliament. Subsequently, in their report the committee of the other place recommended some form of interparliamentary link with the Community parliamentarians. With the approval of both Speakers a letter was sent to the president of the European parliament, signed by the chairmen of both Canadian parliamentary committees dealing with external relations, inviting a delegation to visit Ottawa this fall.
I mentioned that it is perhaps surprising that no formal contact had been made between the two parliaments. It surprises me because the European Community is such a major force in the world today. Canada cannot afford to ignore it even if it wished to do so. Even before its enlargement from six to nine member states earlier this year, the European Community had become the world's largest trading entity. Its imports exceed by a significant amount those of the United States. Canada, as a major trading nation itself, must seek in every possible way to intensify its relations with this new economic giant in Europe.
As those hon. members who participated in the discussions of November 1 will agree, it was a stimulating and informative encounter. Led by Mr. Pierre-Bernard Couste, a vice-president of the European parliament, the delegation was made up of members of all the nine nation states of the community except Ireland and Belgium. However, despite the fact that the various nationalities of the delegates were easily distinguishable, it was clear that this delegation had come to Canada not as representatives of their own countries but as members of a cohesive European parliamentary group with a remarkably homogeneous outlook on the matters under discussion.

Before dealing with the subject matter of the communique, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express on behalf of the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence our deep appreciation to you and your colleague for your co-operation and support that made that visit a success. The committee members were very satisfied with all the arrangements to which your staff co-operated so willingly.

Following the joint meetings of November 1 last, both delegations prepared and approved a release in which they recognized that the links between Canada and the Community could be improved and intensified. Both delegations agreed that periodic meetings should be organized between the European parliament and the Parliament of Canada. Regular contacts would help promote a better understanding and overcome disagreements.
I agree with that statement, Mr. Speaker, but I would go even further. I would like the matter of a regular interparliamentary link rather than periodic meetings to be examined thoroughly. I believe further parliamentary exchanges between both groups would be beneficial and would draw the attention of the European Economic Community on certain Canadian interests, particularly in the area of trade and economy. Indeed, I strongly urge Canada to take the initiative of establishing an interparliamentary link without delay. The report of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee on Canadian Relations with the European Community stated, and I quote:
Delay could result in the build-up by the Community of a network of parliamentary links with third countries' parliaments, leaving the members of the European Parliament with far less inclination or time to consider such links with Canada.
That is the risk involved and pointed out by the Senate committee.
The second point of the statement I wish to discuss especially, Mr. Speaker, concerns the following recommendation:
"that the establishment in Ottawa of an Economic Community delegation, together with an information office, should be considered as a priority by the European Community."
There is no doubt that very few people in Canada are aware of the existence of the European Economic Community and of the part it plays in the changes taking place in Europe. We undoubtedly need a positive information program to explain the Community to Canadians.
This delegation of the European Economic Community in Canada would serve as a link both ways, not only making Canada more aware of the Community and understand it better, but also keeping Brussels informed of Canada's particular interests and points of views.
Mr. Speaker, when thinking of Europe, Canadians are still inclined to recall the old traditional and bilateral relations, namely the relations which we had with France, Belgium, Great Britain and other European countries. From now on, we must learn to imagine new relations, Canadian relations with the European Economic Community. On the other hand, many Europeans have a tendency to consider Canada as an integral part of the North American entity, assuming that they could have with us more or less the same relations that they have with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, to clear up any misunderstanding and dispel any wrong interpretation on both sides, it might be appropriate to hold regular interparliamentary meetings and have a delegation of the Community in Ottawa.
Perhaps it would be interesting and useful to remind hon. members of some facts about the European Parliament. It is often mistaken for the Constituent Assembly of
November 16, 1973

the Council of Europe with which the Canadian Parliament has already had numerous exchanges.
Although the two groups meet in Strasbourg and are formed of Europeans, they have very few points in common. The Council of Europe, made up of 17 member states, is only an advisory body and is mainly concerned with human rights and co-ordination of national regulations and legislation, mostly in the social and cultural fields.
The European Parliament comprises representatives of the national parliaments of the nine member states of the European Economic Community, that is Belgium, Denmark, France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Italy, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.
There are nominally 198 members, although the British Labour Party has until now refused to appoint representatives. That number would increase when the Labour Party decides to send its own delegates. Even though the powers of the European Parliament have so far been of an advisory nature, this organization follows closely the progress of the Community through oral and written questions sent to the Commission, that is the bureaucracy, and to the Council of Ministers. Its powers are increasing and by 1975, it will have acquired budgetary control over administration and information.
In the European Parliament, the debates are conducted in the six languages of the Community members: Danish, Dutch, English, French, German and Italian.
It is interesting to note that members of the European Parliament do not sit by nationality but by party or ideological affiliation. The present parliament is made up of five main groups and a number of non-affiliated members. These main groups are the Christian Democrats, the Socialists, the Liberals and allied members, the Conservatives and the European Democratic Unionists.
The European Parliament meets once a year, mostly in Strasburg, but often in Luxemburg where the secretariat is located. The parliament includes 12 standing committees which meet mostly in Brussels, capital of the European Community.
If one compares the future importance of both groups, that is the European Parliament and the Advisory Assembly of the European Council, I believe it is fair to say that the European Parliament will probably gain in importance. When the Community will have integrated its trade business and can begin integrating its economic and monetary objectives, some form of political integration will most certainly follow.
At the present time, one can only surmise the impact of a political union of Europe on the European Parliament, but it will surely bring about eventually a substantial increase in parliamentary powers and control. Mr. Speaker, I think that this organization will become one of the most important parliaments of the future, and it is in the interest of Canada to establish close relationships with it.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the External Affairs Committee of the Senate on taking the initiative, in the spring of 1973, of making known its intention of meeting with delegates of the European Parliament and of visiting Brussels last March to start discus-
Communique of Canadian and European Parliaments sions with representatives of the various member countries of the European Community. Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the motion I moved on Wednesday was received with so much enthusiasm. I know that several members of the opposition have made known their intention of participating in this debate on the joint statement made public by the delegates of the European Parliament and by those of the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and of the Senate Committee.
For their good work, Mr. Speaker, I want to express to them once more all my gratitude and appreciation.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) for his initiative and the informative and interesting remarks which he has just concluded. I think it is all to the good in this chamber from time to time to take the opportunity to deal with the kind of matters which parliamentary groups have been discussing. If I may say so, I think the other place long ago set a good example on this sort of thing. I commend the hon. member for his initiative and I support completely, thoroughly and most sincerely, the suggestions he has put forward and which are contained in the communique.
One cannot overemphasize the importance of our contacts with and broadening our knowledge of what might be called the new Europe-a new Europe exemplified in the parliament of Europe which the hon. member has so succinctly and so well described. Some of us, although not very old, remember when Europe was a divided Europe with contact points. Now we have developed a Europe which is much more than just a place where other great powers divide and perhaps confront each other explosively. We have seen the era of ostpolotik. I wish the Berlin wall had come down, but in many ways I think it is crumbling and that is to the good. I am very pleased that our country has an ambassador accredited to Brussels. This is a suggestion that I used to make during the past three years. I think on another level this typifies the significance of contact.
It is interesting that in a world of celerity and sophistication in communication, so often we are not really communicating very well. In Canada in the last weeks many people have suddenly awakened to the fact that there is such a world as the Arab world-but it has been there for a long, long time. The new Europe is there, with a tremendous impact and tremendous possibilities. I would like to see us developing the kind of parliamentary arrangements that we have had so long and so successfully with the United States. That is a most excellent group. I hope as parliamentarians we will be in the forefront of developing ties, regularizing contacts and meetings, not with the nation states of Europe-with most of them Canada is not unfamiliar-but with the new Community. This is not a Community which is only economic, but it is a political one in the broadest sense of that expression. So I look forward to the parliamentary exchanges and to our finding more and more opportunities for dialogue with the Community.

November 16, 1973
Communique of Canadian and European Parliaments
While this is a good thing, Mr. Speaker, it is also imperative. I remember not long ago someone appearing before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and saying that perhaps a bigger danger than being taken over economically was being left out when it comes to trade. This statement was made by Mr. Fowler, a prominent member of the Liberal Party who made a thoughtful presentation to the committee. It would be unfortunate in the great world of economic and political giants if we were to find that we had been left out. So it is incumbent upon us to see that this does not happen not only in hard economic terms but in people-to-people contacts.
I am not quite becalmed despite the many assurances that all is going to be well in terms of trade. I do not think we know yet that there will not be ramifications and repercussions that could quite possibly be painful. One thing we do know however-that contacts, associations and friendships should all be stored for the mutual benefit of this country and the community of Europe.
Mr. Speaker, I know that some of my illustrious colleagues also wish to address themselves to this matter, so I simply conclude by quoting from the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) delivered by the eloquent voice of his parliamentary secretary during the visit of the European parliamentarians. He said:
In this context the suggestion of a Canada/European community declaration is attractive. But the determining factor will be substance-not form. Canada is seeking opportunities to develop a dynamic, meaningful and distinctive long term relationship with the European Community. If it is clear that such a declaration can contribute to this objective we will be ready to participate in its elaboration.
With or without a declaration the future evolution of the community's transAtlantic relationship will be of critical interest to Canada. I am confident that common interests and common sense will prevail.
I end as I began, Mr. Speaker, by expressing great pleasure in a debate which was so well launched by my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to emulate the admirable brevity of the last speaker. I, too, would like to commend the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) for his contribution to the debate and his statement about the European Economic Community and Canada's relationships with it. In this party we recognize the value of this interparliamentary encounter. I was one of the delegates who met with the delegation from the European parliament. I agree very much with what I think was one of the key statements in the communique, which was that regular contact would help to promote better understanding and overcome disagreements. The communique provided that this event, which had happened for the first time in history, would be followed by periodic meetings and regular contacts at a later date.
I am reminded, in this connection, that for I think 11 years now representatives of this House and of the Senate have been meeting annually either in Washington or in Ottawa with representatives of the Senate and the House of Representatives of the United States of America. Over the years I think we have come to know each other better. We are very close to the United States, in any event. It seems to me that there is, if not an equal need at least a

clear need for the parliamentarians of Europe, particularly of the nine countries which form the Community, to meet their Canadian counterparts so that we can understand each other's problems and in dealing with each other, as we are bound to do, learn to appreciate each other's problems.
We must recognize the new realities. The European Economic Community is one of the new realities of the world. It is a trading partnership. It is a new political creation, not necessarily like any we have known before. I think, the hon. member for Labelle told us that the Community has a commission which is composed of experts, or what we call permanent members. It has a council of ministers who negotiate, particularly on trading matters, for their particular countries, and it has a European parliament in which all the nine member countries are represented by members designated from the various parties. They meet, I think, about 100 days in the year. It is a truly functioning organization and is likely to grow and change.
We in Canada must recognize the great importance of this Economic Community. I will put a few figures on record. They may be well known to some. They illustrate that for our own prosperity and well-being, we must deal with the Community. The enlarged community has a population in excess of that of the United States, our largest trading partner. The Community's population is 250 million, the people mostly having attained a very high level of civilization and development. The population of the United States is 207 million. The Community has a gross production rate in excess of $700 billion a year. Since the British entry it has become Canada's second largest trading partner. In 1972 the nine member countries bought $2.5 billion of Canadian exports, or 45 per cent of all our exported goods not going to the United States.
In 1972 the Community sold us $2.2 billion worth of goods. The amount of goods imported by the Community is significantly more than the total amount of goods imported by the United States. In 1971 the Community imported over $10 billion worth of finished goods from outside countries. Canada's share was only 1 per cent of this finished product market. The implication for employment in these figures is tremendous. Last year, 1972, Canada lost its traditional balance of trade surplus with the Six and had a trade deficit. So without going into further figures, it is easy to see that the terms of access of Canadian goods and Canadian products into the Economic Community are of the greatest importance.
I think the hon. member for Labelle has already mentioned that there is a great need for having the European Community delegations come to Ottawa so that they may know what is going on here. It is important for Canadians to be made aware of the new Europe. Significantly, the conference which we had was hardly mentioned in the press. I think he Devoir was one of the few newspapers in Canada which thought it worth while noticing the conference. The Globe and Mail of my home town, which calls itself Canada's national newspaper and which used to be one of our best newspapers-I use the past tense deliberately as it no longer covers international affairs as well as it did-said nothing about this unique event. It said nothing about the representatives of the European Community
November 16, 1973

being in this country, although I am informed the newspaper was fully notified of the event. How can Canadians learn to adjust to the realities of the new Europe if events such as this go unnoticed, unattended and unassessed?

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
It is also important for Europeans to distinguish between Canada and the United States. We share the same continent, much of the same culture, and we enjoy a very close and intimate relationship with the United States. For these reasons Europeans sometimes think they need not consider Canada as a separate entity from the United States. They assume that Canadian concerns are similar to those of the United States and that the Economic Community's policies with regard to the United States can apply to Canada as well.
I think it is very much in Canada's interests to mark the differences between ourselves and the United States. The European delegation which came here acknowledged in the joint statement that European Community policies must recognize distinctions and differences between the interests of Canada and those of the United States. The United States and the European Community are already preparing a declaration regarding the principles of their relationships with each other. I think we need a similar statement which would apply to Canada.
The European Community is primarily a trading or economic bloc and as such is of very great importance. I want to mention another factor. No one can foresee exactly what it will grow into. There is every likelihood that it will grow into a more closely knit political organization. The Community now takes part in GATT negotiations on behalf of its nine member nations. This fact in itself shows that the Community is of very great importance. In addition, as I understand it the members of the Economic Community have now said that in the discussions with the United States about a new Atlantic charter they will work together. It is of the utmost importance to consider that although this trading partnership perhaps will not grow into a single state in the foreseeable future, it will grow into a more closely knit political entity with great power and influence in the world and it will act as a counterbalance, if you will, to the two superpowers of the United States and the U.S.S.R.
It behooves us, considering the position we are in, to maintain the closest contact with the European Economic Community, to have the fullest knowledge of it and to show the greatest sympathy for it. That should not be difficult because our links in any event are very close, not only with mother countries such as France and Great Britain but with other countries as well. Many people in Canada come from countries of the European Economic Community. There are very few parts of the world with which we maintain closer historic links.
I close by saying once more that I am glad of the initiative which enabled those of us who were present at the conference to testify to its importance. I express the wish that it will prove to be merely the start of close and growing co-operation between our respective countries.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the previous speakers, I also wish to commend the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) for the motion he has put before the House, which enables us to learn more about the work of the European Parliament and Canada's relations with the European Economic Community. All of us have followed the development of this community and I think the recent meeting is an historic event in a new direction. I feel Canada has shown maturity.
Until now, we used to evolve within a closed circuit with Great Britain and the United States as major partners, and many entertained great fears when Great Britain expressed the wish to join the Common Market.
So as to define the current situation I think we can do no better than look back to see wherefrom those two groups had the idea of meeting today. I was going through the journal International Perspectives when I came across an article by Maurice Torelli which reads as follows: Canada's reaction to Britain's entry into the European Economic Community reveals the basic ambiguity of the Canadian attitude towards the latter; on the one hand, Europe represents the colonial past, the "Land of Sin'' as Jefferson put it, whereas, on the other hand, the EEC, which is the largest trade bloc in a world in which an economy of conglomerates is becoming the rule rather than the exception, is acting more and more as a powerful attractive force. Futurologists a la Herman Kahn speak of the vitality of certain "winning" groups such as Europe or Japan, and of the decline of certain "losing" groups, such as the United States or the U.S.S.R., whose aging administrative structures are beginning to constitute a threat to economic growth. As far as its relationship with these large conglomerates is concerned, Canada, a country that certainly would never have been invented by an economist, is more or less associated with each of them, but the process of becoming a satellite, although it is at a very advanced stage, is not yet complete. This process may be stopped provided Canada adopts a policy consistent with the objectives of national independence and a general increase in prosperity set forth in 1970. In other words, Canada needs a policy of diversification that would make it possible to control the domination of its economy resulting direct-

November 16, 1973
Communique of Canadian and European Parliaments
ly from the very magnitude of its relations with the United States and to find the new markets the structure of its economy requires.
Up to the present, however, Canada, unlike the United States, has not taken Europe seriously; nevertheless, three factors militate in favour of a change of attitude. On the one hand, the end of the war in Vietnam seems for the moment to have checked the observed shift in the economic axis of the developed world Japan exerts a considerable attractive force, but Europe remains clearly the principal economic partner of the United States. On the other hand, Britain's entry into the Common Market puts Canada in a situation similar to that which prevailed after 1846, when Britain abandoned Imperial mercantile protectionism in favour of a system of free exchange, thereby rendering European markets accessible. Because it eliminated the tariff-free importation of Canadian wheat into Britain, the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 was considered in certain Canadian quarters to be a "betrayal" and forced Canada to re-evaluate its general orientation.
This re-evaluation led first of all to the conclusion, in the 1850s, of the Reciprocity Treaty between Canada and the United States, which set up a sort of common market between the two countries for a whole range of products, and then, after the failure of the treaty, to Confederation in 1867. Confederation was the expression of Canada's will for a legal definition of its independence and led to a policy of economic nationalism and to the construction of Canadian transcontinental railways. Canada had decided to find its own identity without either Europe or the United States.
Today, with Britain's entry into the EEC, Canada feels somewhat as though it were the victim of a second British "betrayal"; the end of modern-day preferential treatment by Britain will certainly create difficulties for certain Canadian industries that will be in an unfavourable competitive position on the British market in comparison with the other EEC member states. Canada can opt for a rapprochement with the United States, as it did in 1846, or once again revert to economic nationalism. There is, however, a third solution; it consists in creating closer ties with Europe, the legal terms of which are yet to be defined but whose economic justification may be stated precisely: the third factor that makes Europe particularly interesting for Canada is the complementary nature of the two economies.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to quote part of this article because I think it is partly the prelude of this very recent meeting which has corroborated the ideas of this article's author.
I have here the joint declaration issued at the conclusion of the meeting between the European and Canadian parliamentary delegations. May I quote some parts of it:
Both delegations admitted that there were numerous ways of improving relations between Canada and Europe. For their part, European delegates admitted that EEC policies should take into account distinct interests of Canada and the United States.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the most important points of the present statement which says that, at last, the European Community distinguishes us from the American block, makes a distinction between Canada and the United States, between the Canadian and the American economy and between Canadian and American commerce. I think it is a victory for our representatives here in Canada that they have indicated this approach and have had the European Community make this distinction.
We read further:
Aware, on one hand, of their common interests and ideas and on the other hand, of possible disagreement between Canada and the Community both delegations agreed that periodical meetings should be organized-
-by both Parliaments. And still, this is another argument, it is understood that if we want to remain friends

and to keep up this friendship, there must necessarily be a place of meeting. Then, we spoke of an information office in Canada and of a similar office at the EEC. Such an office is absolutely necessary to be able to discuss all points daily, at each meeting in order to follow the progress of commerce, industry and politics.
Mr. Speaker, we then read:
The extent to which present GATT negotiations will succeed in further liberalizing international trade in industrial and farming products, as well as defining a good behaviour code has been judged of significant importance both for Canada and for the Community.
Mr. Speaker, all the new transactions concerning the western grain, for instance, were conducted mostly on the European market, as Great Britain was the major importer of Quebec cheese. I believe this will open new horizons and broaden for Canada the access to European markets, those of Great Britain as well as of France and other member countries of this community. And if this is good for Europe, I believe it is even better for Canada, because, once more, it shows maturity in opening the door to other markets while breaking away from previous ones, mostly American, without neglecting them for all that.
I believe it is time more than ever before for Canada, as an independent country, to trade with other nations and take its place on the international markets.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre de Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we can say that the constructive dialogue promised by the Nine at their Paris summit in October 1972 is well under way. Owing to various circumstances involving the government, Ottawa has hosted earlier in November large groups of European visitors representing European institutions and the information media the influence of which on the development of our relationship with Europe could not be overestimated.
Whether they were members of the European Economic Council like Sir Christopher Soames, Vice-president and Commissioner for External Affairs of the Council, coming for further discussions with Canadian ministers and officials, or representatives of the European Parliament coming to meet their Canadian counterparts, or representatives of famous newspapers from Western Europe coming to participate to the conference on Canada and the European Community organized by the ICAI with the co-operation of the Department of External Affairs and the European Economic Council, the government was very pleased to welcome them because their visit gave to Europeans and Canadians an exceptional opportunity to discuss the extension and deepening of relationships between Canada and member countries of the European Community. Those discussions should not be short-lived. It is desirable that the dialogue with the European Community be on a permanent basis and with good will that such exchanges of views be frequent and profitable.
It is with the greatest interest that we read the joint statement issued at the meeting between European Parliament delegation and the Canadian Parliament delegation on November 1. The government is encouraged in his own efforts by the positive tone that both parliamentary delegations gave to their discussions on the various items on the orders of the day.
November 16, 1973

The government particularly noticed the recommendation made to draft a statement on the various principles that are to govern the relations between Canada and the European Community. We must be aware that the continuing concern of the government is to ensure that the distinctive Canadian entity in North America, and its own interests and yearnings should be recognized as such by the international community as a whole, and particularly by our European partners, because of the leading part that they are bound to play in the policy of diversification in our external affairs. This means that the matter of a distinct declaration between Canada and the European Economic Community is presently undergoing a thorough examination within the government. Besides, it was already mentioned in a preliminary way with the member countries of the Community. We insist on the fact that in this matter as in others, the material is the most important. What we want is that the relations between Canada and the Community should from now on develop in concrete and dynamic co-operation. If a policy statement could contribute to the achievement of this objective, the government would certainly welcome it.
The joint communique suggests that the European Economic Community ought to give top priority to the establishment in Ottawa of a Community delegation, including an information office. This could not agree more with the views of the government. There cannot be any real communication unless it is bilateral. A European Economic Community mission in Ottawa would be the useful if not essential counterpart of our own permanent delegation to the Community in Brussels. It is certainly not for us to decide which priority should be given by the Community to the establishment of such a mission, but we can only wish that it be top priority.
The government will welcome the full support given by both European and Canadian delegates to freer trade. In fact, it has often stated its policy with regard to freer international trade and it would like it to be even more extensive. It is because we are convinced that such a liberalization would benefit all members of the international community members that we are pleased to see the European Economic Community take such a positive position with regard to a still greater liberalization.
It must be noted that the delegates have acknowledged the common interest that Europeans and Canadians have in cooperating so that Canadian raw materials may be further processed before being exported. This is a major concern of the government. Even if Canada is regarded as an important raw materials supplier, the Canadian people's interests require that these products be further processed before being exported. We would favour for this purpose the development of joint projects with the cooperation of European companies.
Obviously, this question bears a direct relation to that of foreign investment in Canada. The foreign investment review bill established a number of concepts in this regard. It is to be hoped that Europeans may continue to invest in Canada with tangible benefits for the Canadian economy.
Communique of Canadian and European Parliaments
In this time of fast development on both sides of the Atlantic, it is important to remember, even if it is a truism, that as important as it is, the economic side of our relations with the EEC is not the only one to be considered, nor even the one that matters most. On this point, it is pleasant for us, but also greatly significant, that the European delegation has expressed its satisfaction over the constructive role played by Canada as concerns the CSCE. That part of the statement clearly shows that Canada is pursuing vital objectives in Europe, and it recognizes that the security of Canada cannot be separated from that of Europe and that bonds of all kinds, made through our history, origins and common ideals, encompass and surpass our respective policies for the greater prosperity of all concerned.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to join with the previous speakers in congratulating the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) who introduced the motion which is now before us. [English]
That was at your initiative, Mr. Speaker, having so graciously suggested that we table the communique of this meeting. With your permission I should like to enlarge the debate slightly, taking this as a point of departure. I should like to formulate a plea which has both historical and parliamentary overtones. What I want to see is a regular record of the meetings which parliamentarians attend, whether they be here or overseas. The latest example of such a meeting has just closed its formal gathering with a luncheon today. I am not suggesting that we try to put on the record of Hansard all the proceedings, but at least the agenda of the matters that were covered.
I should like to go back a bit in history and indicate just what is the degree of record we have of these various gatherings. I went back as far as 1959 because I had a direct interest in the initial proceedings of the Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group. At that time we managed to have tabled the record of the first meeting of the Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group. That followed through sequentially year after year until about 1966. For some reason not clear from the record, we did not manage to carry on. There was a break in 1966, and then in 1970 the Clerk of the House laid upon the table copies of the report of the thirteenth meeting of the Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group. I submit that is not good enough. Some of us in this House were chosen as delegates to this international gathering. We cannot all be there, but when we come back from such meetings we should be able to at least table the record here so that those who were not privileged to attend the meetings would know what we were doing. The Canadian public should know also.
I have been extremely fortunate in the short time I have been a member of this parliament to have attended no less than four of these meetings. One was in Bonn, before this session first convened, of the North Atlantic assembly. Unfortunately, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) is not here; I was going to refer to something of interest to him. I also attended in July a meeting of the international parliamentary group in Washington. This was a very important one for me because the main problem discussed was the movement of tankers through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. I was also a Canadian member at

There was an exchange of ideas to our mutual benefit, and that is a great thing. But more than being to our mutual intellectual benefit, it was to our mutual political benefit in the context that we were able to meet with our fellow parliamentarians and legislators across the country and discuss questions of importance to us.
I regret, as I said, that the hon. member for Laprairie is not here as this is one of the strange anomalies of tabling various reports. He was charged at the North Atlantic assembly with preparing a report on the fisheries of the North Atlantic. He did so and tabled it at the fisheries committee. It is there among parliamentary records, but it should be on Hansard. It is my plea that before too long we shall be able to proceed in this way in the normal course of

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not by any stretch of the imagination want to take up very much time, except I have an idea- which is perhaps a bit dangerous-that if we really mean what we say in this most interesting hour of debate, and I really think we do, one way it might be accomplished is for us as a parliament, if the government cannot do it, to persuade the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on an urgent basis-I am very serious-to visit first of all Brussels to ensure that the Canadian public and this parliament understands the importance of the link between the old Europe, which has sort of been reincarnated in the European Community, with Canada and also to visit other European countries. I have been here as long as the Prime Minister and I must say I did not think it would be so hard to get the right hon. gentleman to travel. I hope that if he or his advisers have time to read the remarks which have been made in the last hour there will be an understanding of the serious urgency of having the Prime Minister of Canada visit Brussels.
My own leader made such a visit in 1970, well before an ambassador was nominated for the special post of ambassador to the Community. I think in all the travel plans the Prime Minister has, none can be so urgent as a visit first to Brussels and, hopefully, to other countries of the Community. If invitations are wanted, of course they can be easily obtained. I hope this whole idea will go forward quickly.

subsubtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY REPRESENTATIVES OF CANADIAN AND EUROPEAN PARLIAMENTS
speechtext:
I sense that the House has met the objective raised by the hon. Member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) in presenting his motion on Wednesday, November 14. Accordingly, the hour for private members' business has expired. It being five o'clock, this House stands adjourned until Monday next at 2 p.m.
At five o'clock the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
November 16, 1973

A delegation from the European Community's Parliament today held the first formal meeting with members of the Canadian Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House of Commons Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
The two delegations recognized that much could be done to improve Canada-Community relations. The Canadian delegation welcomed the specific mention of Canada in the Paris summit meeting communique as a country with which the Community should maintain "a constructive dialogue". For their part, the European delegates acknowledged that EC policies must recognize the distinction between the interests of Canada and the United States. To this end all delegates agreed that a separate EC-Canada dialogue should be maintained. Taking note of the proposed US-EC declaration, the delegations further recommended that a separate declaration of principles be drawn up for Canada-EC relations.
Conscious on the one hand of the common interests and perceptions they share and, on the other, of the areas of potential disagreement that could arise between Canada and the Community both delegations agreed that periodic meetings should be organized between the European Parliament and the Parliament of Canada. Regular contact would help to promote better understanding and overcome disagreements.
The necessity for an EC institutional channel in Canada capable of two-way communication was recognized by the Parliamentarians of both sides. It was agreed that the establishment in Ottawa of an EC Delegation including an Information Office should be given the very highest priority by the Community.
In respect to general EC-Canada trade relations, Canadian members stressed the commitment which Canada felt to a truly multilateral trading system and their apprehension over the possibility of the major trading groupings becoming inward-looking. Such a development would run counter to the efforts of both Canada and the Community to diversify their economic and other relations. The success of the current GATT negotiations in further liberalizing international trade in industrial and agricultural products and in reaching agreement on trade conduct was considered to be of great importance both to Canada and to the Community. The delegates of the European Parliament stressed that both their own policy and also the overriding necessities of the Community's economy made trade liberalization a major priority for them. The whole recent history of the Community, and also the very high degree of trade liberalization which the Community had already achieved was evidence of this policy.
The European delegates expressed their appreciation of the constructive role Canada is playing in the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
The two delegations recognized that although Canada was an oil-exporting as well as an oil-importing nation, it confronted many of the same problems the Community faced. The delegates concluded that methods for co-operation exploration and development of oil sources in the North Atlantic and Eastern Arctic and the Alberta tar-sands could be profitably examined. The two delegations recognized the great importance of co-operation in the field of scientific research and technology. The European parliamentarians underlined their interest in the results obtained in Canada in the field of nuclear reactors.
In addition, it was agreed that co-operation between member states of the Community and Canada in the upgrading of industrial raw materials could be mutually advantageous. Canada, a major supplier of primary products to the Community, was interested in joint ventures with European companies to develop further processing of its industrial raw materials before export. For their part, some member states of the Community were interested to ensure future supplies through such joint undertakings.
The Community is Canada's largest export market for agricultural products (35%). Canadian export sales to the European Community itself as well as to third markets are affected by the CAP system of support prices-e.g. for barley. British entry has meant that the impact of the CAP is being felt even more deeply. However, the Canadian parliamentarians recognized the important social and political significance of the Community's agricultural policy.
In discussing foreign investment in Europe and Canada, the two sides agreed that there were increasingly interesting investment possibilities between the member states of the Community and Canada in both directions. The delegates expressed the hope that such reciprocal investment projects would increase, whilst recognizing that the question of multinational corporations would inevitably have to be examined.
The European and Canadian parliamentarians, while recognizing the significance of their respective aid policies, agreed on the need to take more energetic action in implementing their responsibilities to developing countries.
